turns.content: An n by n by n cube is divided into unit cubes and colored. Call the n slices perpendicular to the three coordinate axes x-, y-, and z-slices. The set of colors in every slice must also occur as the color set of a slice in each other orientation. Restate the quantity to maximize and the exact matching condition. Note that the condition does not require the coloring to be invariant under every permutation of coordinates.

Develop a counting strategy that can prove an upper bound and also suggest a coloring that attains it. In particular, consider grouping colors by how many unit cubes carry them and explain what must be counted.

Begin the upper-bound argument. Fix an x-slice X and choose a y-slice Y and z-slice Z with the same color set. Analyze the case in which X contains a color used on exactly one cube, and derive the resulting local bound involving colors used once or twice.
Handle the complementary case in which X contains no color used on exactly one cube. Derive the corresponding local estimate and compare it with the bound from the previous case.
Sum the local bound over all x-slices. Combine it with the total number n^3 of unit cubes and the multiplicities of the color classes to obtain a global upper bound on the number of colors.

For a construction meeting the bound, label each cube by (x,y,z) in {1,...,n}^3. Define color classes for the diagonal cubes and for coordinate triples containing exactly two distinct values, and check how these classes appear in slices of different orientations.

For three distinct indices i<j<k, partition the six coordinate permutations into as many valid color classes as possible. Describe the grouping and explain why it preserves the required slice matching.
Verify that the construction now gives every x-slice a y-slice and a z-slice with the same color set, and likewise after cyclically exchanging the orientations.
Count the singleton, two-value, and three-value color classes in this construction, then simplify their total as a function of n.
Compare the construction count with the upper bound. What is the maximal possible number of colors?
